subject: SLA exception request — content filter & tool-calling timeouts
messages:
From: Maya Singh <maya@acme.ai>
To: karthik_iyer@redwood.ai, Acme AI Procurement <procurement@acme.ai>
Date: Tue, 28 Jul 2026 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: SLA exception request — content filter & tool-calling timeouts

Hi Karthik / Procurement team,

We're seeing a recurring class of incidents in the last two weeks post-integration that I wanted to surface formally so procurement/legal can get an exception captured in the SOW. Summary: when the content filter pipeline experiences elevated latency (typically during peak traffic or when the filter model scales up), downstream tool-calls (webhook invocations and structured output extraction) are timing out, producing failed responses for our end users. We recorded three production incidents (logs attached) where the end-to-end user-facing request failed while Redwood's baseline model serving remained up.

What we need:
- Explicit carve-out language that excludes "filter-induced latency" and resultant tool-call timeouts from uptime/availability calculations for the primary model endpoint, OR an alternative contractual remedy (e.g., credit/repair SLAs for those incidents).
- A tolerance for longer tool-call timeouts in our integration (we are asking for up to 20s for tool-calls triggered by content-filtering flows) while you implement any longer-term runtime mitigations.
- Clear metrics and measurement method so both sides can validate incidents (e.g., a metric name and a single-tenant log format we can reference).

Attached: incident-logs-20260726.zip (contains traces and sample requests).

Timeline: our legal/procurement team needs proposed contracting language by end-of-day Thursday (2026-07-29) to keep our procurement timeline. Please let me know if you need more incident context or if you'd prefer a short call.

Thanks,
Maya Singh

Hi Maya — thanks for the clear summary and the diagnostics. We took a first pass through the attached logs. Acknowledged — the incidents you described look like content-filter scaling events that add variable latency before tool dispatch.

Next steps from our side:
- I'll loop in Product & Legal (cc'd Marissa for Product) to draft specific carve-out language.
- Short-term mitigations we can enable ASAP: 1) allow a lightweight fast-path filter for high-throughput requests (reduces filtering latency), 2) suggest increasing client-side tool-call timeout to 20s as you requested, and 3) enable aggressive retry with jitter for idempotent tool-calls. We can flip these via feature flag within 24–48 hours.

I've attached an initial proposal (proposed-sla-carveout.docx) that Marissa is reviewing internally. Can we lock a 30-min call tomorrow to walk the language? I can do 10–10:30am PT or 3–3:30pm PT.

Subject: Internal: proposed carve-out wording and metrics

Karthik / Rishi —

Quick technical note on draft language. I reviewed the logs and our instrumentation. The carve-out should be tightly scoped so it only applies to filtering and tool-dispatch paths, not general runtime or kernel-level failures. Proposed measurable definition and clause below — happy to iterate.

Proposed measurable definition (so both legal teams can reference the same signal):
- "Filter-induced latency incident": any user request where the per-request filter latency (metric: redwood.filter.latency_ms, p99 over request) exceeds 1500ms AND where a downstream tool-call times out or returns an error within 30s.
- Measurement window: incidents are counted per 5-minute window; qualifying incidents must be reproducible in single-tenant trace logs or via provided request ids.

Sample contract clause (draft):
"Filter & Tool-Call Exception: Notwithstanding Section 3 (Service Availability), periods during which Redwood's content-filtering subsystem experiences elevated latency that leads to tool-calling timeouts (as measured by the agreed metric redwood.filter.latency_ms and documented per-request traces) shall not be counted against Redwood's Service Availability calculations. Such exceptions are limited to events that meet the agreed definition and are subject to the remedies set forth in Appendix B (Filtered-Request Mitigations)."

Operational guardrails I recommend including:
- Cap the carve-out to no more than 4 incidents (as defined) per rolling 30-day period.
- Require post-incident analysis and a remediation plan within 5 business days for any qualifying incident.
- Provide Acme with access to a filtered subset of request traces for the purpose of audit (redacted PII).

If we accept those measurements and guardrails, we can map the clause to a monitoring dashboard and create an automated incident report we can share.

Marissa Cole
Director, Product — Inference & Reliability
Redwood Inference

Maya — thanks for your patience. Per our internal review we've put together proposed language and operational guardrails to address your procurement ask. Please see attached redlines and the short summary below.

Summary of proposed approach (high level):
- Scope: carve-out applies only to filter-induced latency incidents (definition attached). It does NOT apply to general model-serving runtime failures, network connectivity, or capacity outages.
- Measurement: incidents are measured by the agreed metric redwood.filter.latency_ms (p99) plus documented per-request trace evidence.
- Limits & remediation: carve-outs are limited to 4 qualifying incidents per rolling 30-day window; for any qualifying incident Redwood will provide a written RCA and remediation plan within 5 business days.
- Short-term mitigations: we will enable the fast-path filter and increase client-side tool-call timeout to 20s for your integration on Monday, 2026-08-02 (configurable per-route).

Attachments: acme-sla-redlines.pdf, proposed-sla-carveout.docx

If that aligns, can Procurement confirm the clause with legal and confirm whether they want the carve-out added to Appendix B (preferred) or directly to Section 3 of the SOW? We are available for a 30-min sync tomorrow at 10am PT.
